climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Plastic was invented in the early 20th century as a cheap, versatile material that could be molded into almost anything. Mass production took off after World War II, and annual output now exceeds 400 million tonnes. Most plastic ever made still exists because it takes hundreds of years to degrade.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Plastic's durability, the same quality that makes it useful, makes it an environmental nightmare. Understanding its origins clarifies why managing plastic waste is so difficult.
takeaways: Annual global plastic production exceeds 400 million tonnes
Most plastic ever made still exists in some form
Plastic takes hundreds of years to break down in nature

faq.question: When was plastic first mass-produced?
faq.answer: Bakelite, the first truly synthetic plastic, was invented in 1907. Mass production of plastics like polyethylene and PVC exploded in the 1950s. Since then, global annual production has grown from about 2 million tonnes to over 400 million tonnes.

faq.question: How long does plastic take to decompose?
faq.answer: Estimates range from 20 years for a thin plastic bag to over 500 years for a plastic bottle. Plastic does not truly biodegrade but fragments into smaller and smaller microplastics that persist in the environment indefinitely.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Single-use plastics like bags, straws, cutlery, and packaging are used for minutes but persist in the environment for centuries. They make up roughly 40 percent of all plastic produced and are the most common items found in ocean and beach cleanups worldwide.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Banning or reducing single-use plastics is one of the quickest wins against plastic pollution. Many countries and cities have already begun phase-outs with measurable results.
takeaways: Single-use items make up about 40 percent of plastic production
They are the most common debris in ocean and beach cleanups
Over 120 countries have enacted bans on some single-use plastics

faq.question: Which single-use plastics are banned most often?
faq.answer: Plastic bags, straws, stirrers, cutlery, and expanded polystyrene food containers are the most commonly banned items. The European Union's Single-Use Plastics Directive, enacted in 2021, banned the top 10 items found on European beaches.

faq.question: Do single-use plastic bans actually reduce pollution?
faq.answer: Yes. Countries with bag bans or fees have seen plastic bag litter drop by 40 to 90 percent. Kenya's strict 2017 bag ban dramatically reduced visible plastic pollution. Effectiveness depends on enforcement and the availability of affordable alternatives.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a massive accumulation of plastic debris in the North Pacific, covering an area roughly three times the size of France. It consists mostly of microplastics suspended in the water column rather than a visible island, making cleanup extremely challenging.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: The garbage patch symbolizes the global plastic pollution crisis. Its existence demonstrates how ocean currents concentrate waste from every continent into persistent marine debris zones.
takeaways: The patch covers about 1.6 million square kilometers
It consists mostly of tiny microplastics, not visible debris
Ocean currents trap and concentrate floating plastic waste

faq.question: Can the Great Pacific Garbage Patch be cleaned up?
faq.answer: Organizations like The Ocean Cleanup are deploying floating barriers to collect surface debris. However, the vast scale and predominance of microplastics make complete removal nearly impossible. Preventing plastic from entering the ocean in the first place is far more effective.

faq.question: Are there other garbage patches in the ocean?
faq.answer: Yes. Ocean gyres in the North Atlantic, South Pacific, South Atlantic, and Indian Ocean all have accumulated plastic debris zones. Every ocean basin has one, though the North Pacific patch is the largest and most studied.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than five millimeters found in oceans, rivers, soil, food, and even human blood. They originate from degrading larger plastics, synthetic clothing fibers, tire wear, and industrial processes. Their ubiquity raises growing concerns about long-term health and ecosystem impacts.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Microplastics have infiltrated every environment on Earth, including human bodies. The full health implications are still unknown, making this a major emerging environmental and health concern.
takeaways: Microplastics are found in water, soil, air, and human tissue
Synthetic clothing and tire wear are major sources
Health effects of chronic exposure are still being studied

faq.question: How do microplastics enter the human body?
faq.answer: Through drinking water, food especially seafood, and inhaled air. Studies have detected microplastics in human blood, lungs, liver, and placentas. Bottled water contains more microplastics than tap water due to leaching from plastic containers.

faq.question: Can microplastics be filtered out of water?
faq.answer: Conventional water treatment removes some microplastics but not all. Advanced filtration like activated carbon and ultrafiltration membranes are more effective. Washing machine filters can capture synthetic fibers at the source before they enter wastewater.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Over 700 marine species are known to be harmed by plastic pollution through entanglement, ingestion, or habitat damage. Sea turtles mistake bags for jellyfish, seabirds feed plastic to their chicks, and whales have been found dead with stomachs full of plastic waste.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Plastic is killing marine wildlife at industrial scale. The emotional and ecological impact drives public demand for action on plastic pollution and ocean conservation.
takeaways: Over 700 marine species are affected by plastic pollution
Ingestion and entanglement are the primary threats
Plastic enters marine food chains at every trophic level

faq.question: How many marine animals die from plastic each year?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest over 100,000 marine mammals and one million seabirds die annually from plastic ingestion or entanglement. The true number is likely much higher because most deaths go unobserved in the open ocean.

faq.question: How does plastic enter marine food chains?
faq.answer: Tiny organisms ingest microplastics, which are then consumed by small fish, and so on up the food chain. Toxins adsorbed onto plastic surfaces concentrate at each level. Humans eating seafood are at the top of this chain.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Modern sanitary landfills are engineered to contain waste with clay and synthetic liners, leachate collection systems, and methane capture infrastructure. They represent a massive improvement over open dumps, but they still release greenhouse gases, occupy valuable land, and risk leaking toxins into groundwater.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Landfills remain the primary destination for waste in most countries. Understanding how they work reveals both their necessity and the urgency of reducing the waste that fills them.
takeaways: Modern landfills use liners and leachate collection systems
Decomposing waste produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas
Even engineered landfills pose long-term contamination risks

faq.question: How do landfills produce methane?
faq.answer: Organic waste like food and paper decomposes anaerobically underground, producing methane. Landfills are the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions globally. Gas capture systems can collect methane for energy, but many landfills lack this infrastructure.

faq.question: How long do landfill liners last?
faq.answer: Synthetic liners are designed to last 30 to 50 years, but landfill contents remain hazardous for centuries. Over time, liners can crack, shift, or degrade, allowing leachate containing heavy metals and chemicals to seep into groundwater. Perpetual monitoring is required.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Landfills produce roughly 11 percent of global methane emissions as organic waste decomposes without oxygen. Methane is over 80 times more potent than CO2 as a greenhouse gas over 20 years. Capturing landfill gas for energy reduces emissions while producing electricity or heat.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Cutting landfill methane is one of the fastest ways to slow near-term warming. Diverting organic waste from landfills and capturing gas from existing sites offer immediate climate benefits.
takeaways: Landfills produce about 11 percent of global methane emissions
Methane is over 80 times more potent than CO2 over 20 years
Gas capture converts methane into usable energy

faq.question: How is landfill gas captured?
faq.answer: Vertical wells and horizontal collectors are drilled into the waste mass to extract gas under vacuum. The collected methane is either burned in engines to generate electricity, processed to pipeline-quality natural gas, or flared to convert it to the less potent CO2.

faq.question: Would composting eliminate landfill methane?
faq.answer: Diverting all organic waste to composting or anaerobic digestion would dramatically reduce landfill methane because organics are the primary source. Studies suggest this could cut landfill emissions by 50 to 70 percent in countries with high food waste.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Waste incineration burns garbage at high temperatures, reducing its volume by up to 90 percent and generating electricity or heat. Modern incinerators use advanced filters to limit air pollution. However, they still emit CO2, can discourage recycling, and face public opposition over health concerns.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Incineration is a major waste strategy in Europe and Japan but remains controversial. Understanding its trade-offs is essential for designing waste systems that minimize both pollution and landfill dependence.
takeaways: Incineration reduces waste volume by up to 90 percent
Energy recovery generates electricity and district heating
It still emits CO2 and can disincentivize recycling

faq.question: Is waste incineration cleaner than landfilling?
faq.answer: Modern incinerators emit less methane than landfills and reduce waste volume dramatically. However, they emit CO2 and trace pollutants, and their climate footprint depends on what is burned. Plastics release fossil carbon, while organic waste is closer to carbon neutral.

faq.question: Which countries incinerate the most waste?
faq.answer: Japan, Denmark, Sweden, and Singapore incinerate a high share of waste with energy recovery. Denmark generates about 5 percent of its electricity from waste incineration. Sweden imports waste from other countries to feed its waste-to-energy plants.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: About 40 percent of the world's waste is disposed of in open dumps, with no liners, leachate collection, or gas capture. These sites contaminate groundwater, poison surrounding communities, and release uncontrolled methane. Open dumping is concentrated in low-income countries with limited waste infrastructure.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Open dumps are the worst form of waste disposal, posing severe health and environmental risks. Closing them and transitioning to managed systems is critical for global waste management.
takeaways: About 40 percent of global waste goes to open dumps
No environmental controls protect surrounding communities
Dump fires release toxic smoke and carcinogens

faq.question: How do open dumps affect nearby communities?
faq.answer: Residents suffer from toxic smoke when waste burns, contaminated water from leaching chemicals, disease spread by scavenging animals and insects, and respiratory illness from airborne pollutants. Those living closest, often the poorest, bear the heaviest health burden.

faq.question: What does it cost to close an open dump?
faq.answer: Costs vary enormously, but transitioning from open dumping to sanitary landfill or alternative systems requires investment in site remediation, new collection infrastructure, and ongoing operational funding. International financing and technical assistance are often essential.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Wealthy countries have long exported millions of tonnes of plastic, paper, and electronic waste to developing nations for processing or disposal. China's 2018 ban on waste imports disrupted this trade, revealing that many exporting countries had not built adequate domestic recycling capacity.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: The waste trade offloads environmental burdens onto poorer countries. Understanding it exposes inequities in global waste management and the need for domestic recycling infrastructure.
takeaways: Wealthy nations ship millions of tonnes of waste abroad
China's 2018 import ban disrupted the global waste trade
Many exporting countries lack domestic recycling capacity

faq.question: Why did China ban waste imports?
faq.answer: China received about half the world's recyclable waste for decades, but contamination rates were rising. The National Sword policy banned 24 categories of waste imports to protect domestic health and environment, forcing exporting countries to handle their own waste.

faq.question: Where does waste go now that China has closed its doors?
faq.answer: Exports shifted to Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, Vietnam, and Indonesia, which quickly became overwhelmed and imposed their own restrictions. Some waste is now landfilled or incinerated domestically. The disruption has spurred investment in local recycling capacity.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Global recycling rates remain far lower than most people assume. Only about 9 percent of all plastic ever produced has been recycled, and actual recycling rates for mixed municipal waste in many countries hover around 20 to 30 percent. Contamination, market economics, and infrastructure gaps limit progress.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Believing that recycling is solving the waste problem creates false confidence. Honest assessment of recycling rates reveals the urgent need for waste reduction, better systems, and producer responsibility.
takeaways: Only about 9 percent of all plastic ever made has been recycled
Contamination renders much collected recyclable material unusable
Recycling alone cannot solve the waste crisis

faq.question: Why is the plastic recycling rate so low?
faq.answer: There are thousands of plastic types, many of which cannot be economically recycled. Contamination with food or mixed materials degrades quality. Virgin plastic is often cheaper than recycled. Collection infrastructure is limited outside wealthy countries.

faq.question: Which materials are actually recycled at high rates?
faq.answer: Aluminum cans have recycling rates above 70 percent in many countries because recycling aluminum uses 95 percent less energy than producing new metal. Steel and cardboard also recycle well. Glass and some paper grades achieve moderate rates depending on local infrastructure.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Plastic recycling faces fundamental barriers: thousands of polymer types that cannot be mixed, contamination that degrades quality, downcycling into lower-value products, and market conditions that make virgin plastic cheaper. These systemic problems mean most plastic placed in recycling bins is never truly recycled.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: The recycling symbol on plastic packaging creates an illusion of sustainability. Understanding why plastic recycling fails drives support for reduction, reuse, and systemic redesign.
takeaways: Different plastic types cannot be mixed in recycling
Recycled plastic is usually downcycled to lower-value uses
Virgin plastic is often cheaper than recycled plastic

faq.question: What is downcycling?
faq.answer: Downcycling converts a material into a lower-quality product that cannot be recycled again. A plastic bottle might become synthetic carpet fiber, which then goes to landfill. True closed-loop recycling where a bottle becomes a new bottle is rare for most plastics.

faq.question: Is chemical recycling the solution for plastic?
faq.answer: Chemical recycling breaks plastic back into its molecular building blocks, theoretically allowing infinite recycling. However, most facilities are still experimental, energy-intensive, and not yet economical at scale. It may complement but not replace waste reduction strategies.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Aluminum can be recycled indefinitely without losing quality, making it one of the most circular materials in existence. Recycling aluminum uses only 5 percent of the energy required to produce new aluminum from bauxite ore. Despite this, global collection rates still leave billions of cans unrecycled each year.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Aluminum proves that true circular material flows are possible. Its recycling success offers a model for other materials and highlights what strong collection systems can achieve.
takeaways: Aluminum can be recycled infinitely without quality loss
Recycling saves 95 percent of the energy of new production
Nearly 75 percent of all aluminum ever produced is still in use

faq.question: Why is aluminum recycling so energy efficient?
faq.answer: Smelting new aluminum from bauxite ore requires enormous electricity for electrolysis. Remelting existing aluminum takes a fraction of that energy because the atomic bonds are already formed. This makes recycled aluminum profoundly cheaper and lower-carbon.

faq.question: What is the global aluminum can recycling rate?
faq.answer: Global rates vary from over 90 percent in Brazil and Germany, where deposit systems exist, to under 50 percent in countries without them. Deposit-return schemes dramatically boost collection rates because cans have redeemable cash value.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Composting converts food scraps, yard waste, and other organic matter into nutrient-rich soil amendment through controlled biological decomposition. It diverts waste from landfills, eliminates methane emissions from anaerobic decay, and produces a product that enriches soil and helps retain water.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Organic waste is the largest component of landfill by weight and the primary source of landfill methane. Composting is a proven, scalable solution with immediate climate benefits.
takeaways: Composting prevents methane that organic waste would produce in landfills
The finished product enriches soil and improves water retention
Organics are the largest category of landfilled waste by weight

faq.question: What can be composted?
faq.answer: Food scraps, yard trimmings, coffee grounds, eggshells, paper towels, and cardboard can all be composted. Meat and dairy can be composted in industrial facilities that reach high temperatures but are usually avoided in home composting due to odor and pest concerns.

faq.question: How does composting reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
faq.answer: In landfills, organic matter decomposes without oxygen, producing methane. Composting provides oxygen so microbes produce CO2 instead, which is 80 times less potent as a greenhouse gas. The resulting compost also sequesters some carbon in soil.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Bioplastics are made from plant-based materials instead of fossil fuels and are sometimes designed to be biodegradable or compostable. However, most bioplastics do not break down in natural environments, contaminate conventional recycling streams, and still require significant land and resources to produce.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Bioplastics are marketed as green alternatives, but the reality is more complex. Misleading claims can divert attention from the more important goal of reducing overall plastic use.
takeaways: Bioplastics come from plant sources rather than petroleum
Most require industrial composting and do not degrade in nature
They contaminate conventional plastic recycling streams

faq.question: Do bioplastics break down in the ocean?
faq.answer: Most bioplastics do not degrade in marine environments. They require specific industrial composting conditions with high temperatures and controlled moisture. In the ocean, they behave much like conventional plastic, persisting and harming marine life.

faq.question: Are bioplastics better for the environment than regular plastic?
faq.answer: It depends on the full lifecycle. Some bioplastics have lower carbon footprints in production but require agricultural land and water. If they end up in landfill rather than industrial composters, their environmental advantage largely disappears.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Roughly one-third of all food produced globally is wasted, amounting to about 1.3 billion tonnes per year. In wealthy countries, most waste occurs at the retail and consumer level, while in developing nations it happens during harvest, storage, and transport due to infrastructure limitations.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Food waste squanders the water, energy, land, and labor used in production and generates enormous greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing it is one of the most impactful climate actions available.
takeaways: About one-third of global food production is wasted annually
Food waste in landfills generates significant methane emissions
Wealthy nations waste most food at the consumer level

faq.question: How much greenhouse gas does food waste produce?
faq.answer: If food waste were a country, it would be the third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases after the US and China. Rotting food in landfills produces methane, and the wasted resources embedded in growing, transporting, and refrigerating uneaten food add significantly more.

faq.question: Why do wealthy countries waste so much food?
faq.answer: Abundance, aesthetic standards that reject imperfect produce, confusing date labels, large portion sizes, and low food costs relative to income all contribute. Consumers in wealthy countries waste more per capita because the financial motivation to avoid waste is weak.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Food waste accounts for roughly 8 to 10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions when including production, transport, and decomposition in landfills. Reducing food waste is ranked among the top climate solutions by Project Drawdown because it cuts emissions while saving resources and feeding more people.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Cutting food waste requires no new technology and delivers immediate climate, economic, and humanitarian benefits. It is one of the most accessible climate solutions for individuals and businesses.
takeaways: Food waste produces 8 to 10 percent of global emissions
Project Drawdown ranks food waste reduction as a top solution
Reducing waste also saves water, land, and economic resources

faq.question: What is the link between food waste and methane?
faq.answer: When food decomposes in oxygen-deprived landfill conditions, it produces methane rather than CO2. Methane is over 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas over 20 years. Diverting food to composting or anaerobic digestion captures or avoids this methane.

faq.question: What can individuals do to reduce food waste?
faq.answer: Plan meals and shop with a list, store food properly to extend freshness, understand date labels, use leftovers creatively, compost scraps that cannot be eaten, and buy imperfect produce. Household changes alone could significantly reduce total food waste.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Food is lost at every stage from farm to fork. In developing countries, poor storage, unreliable transport, and lack of cold chains cause most losses at the production stage. In wealthy countries, supermarket rejection of imperfect produce and consumer behavior drive waste at the end of the chain.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Addressing food waste requires different solutions at different points in the supply chain. Targeting the biggest loss points in each context maximizes impact and resource savings.
takeaways: Developing nations lose food mainly during harvest and storage
Wealthy nations waste food at retail and consumer stages
Cold chain infrastructure reduces post-harvest loss dramatically

faq.question: What is a cold chain?
faq.answer: A cold chain is an unbroken series of refrigerated storage and transport links that keeps perishable food at safe temperatures from harvest to consumer. In many developing countries, lack of cold chain infrastructure causes up to 40 percent of food to spoil before it reaches market.

faq.question: Why do supermarkets reject so much produce?
faq.answer: Retailers enforce strict cosmetic standards: odd shapes, small sizes, or minor blemishes lead to rejection even though the food is perfectly safe and nutritious. This drives enormous waste at the farm level. The ugly food movement works to change these norms.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Date labels like best before, sell by, and use by confuse consumers into discarding safe food. Best before indicates peak quality, not safety. Studies suggest that date label confusion contributes to roughly 10 percent of food waste in Europe, as people throw away food that is still perfectly edible.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Standardizing and clarifying date labels is a simple policy change that could prevent millions of tonnes of unnecessary food waste and associated emissions each year.
takeaways: Best before indicates quality, not safety
Date label confusion causes about 10 percent of EU food waste
Standardizing labels could prevent millions of tonnes of waste

faq.question: What is the difference between best before and use by?
faq.answer: Best before indicates when food is at peak quality but is still generally safe to eat after that date. Use by marks the last date food is considered safe to consume, typically applied to highly perishable items like raw meat and dairy.

faq.question: How can date label reform reduce food waste?
faq.answer: Eliminating or simplifying sell by and best before dates, educating consumers about what labels mean, and encouraging sensory checks before discarding food could all help. Some countries are already removing best before dates from long-lasting products like pasta and rice.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The ugly food movement fights food waste by promoting the sale and consumption of cosmetically imperfect produce. Initiatives include discounted ugly produce boxes, relaxed supermarket appearance standards, and campaigns that challenge the expectation that fruits and vegetables must look picture-perfect.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Up to 40 percent of produce is discarded for purely cosmetic reasons. The ugly food movement addresses a massive source of waste by changing perceptions rather than technology.
takeaways: Up to 40 percent of produce is rejected for cosmetic defects
Ugly produce subscriptions sell imperfect food at discount
Changing consumer expectations directly reduces farm-level waste

faq.question: Is ugly produce as nutritious as perfect-looking produce?
faq.answer: Yes. Shape, size, and surface blemishes have no effect on nutritional content or taste. An oddly shaped carrot or a spotted apple provides the same vitamins, minerals, and fiber as its cosmetically perfect counterpart.

faq.question: How successful are ugly produce programs?
faq.answer: Companies like Imperfect Foods and services from major retailers have diverted millions of kilograms of produce from waste. France pioneered intermarche's inglorious fruits and vegetables campaign, which went viral and inspired similar efforts worldwide.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The world generates over 62 million tonnes of electronic waste per year, and less than 20 percent is formally recycled. Discarded phones, computers, and appliances contain valuable metals like gold, copper, and rare earths, but also hazardous materials like lead, mercury, and cadmium.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: E-waste is the fastest growing waste stream globally. It represents both a massive resource loss and a toxic threat when improperly handled in developing countries.
takeaways: Over 62 million tonnes of e-waste is generated annually
Less than 20 percent is formally recycled worldwide
E-waste contains both valuable and hazardous materials

faq.question: What valuable materials are in e-waste?
faq.answer: A tonne of circuit boards contains roughly 800 times more gold than a tonne of gold ore. E-waste also contains copper, silver, palladium, platinum, and rare earth elements. The total value of raw materials in global e-waste exceeds $60 billion annually.

faq.question: Why is so little e-waste recycled?
faq.answer: Recycling electronics is complex and costly, requiring specialized dismantling. Many consumers hoard old devices or throw them in regular trash. Collection systems are inadequate, and informal recyclers in developing countries process e-waste unsafely for quick profit.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Rare earth minerals essential for electronics, batteries, and renewable energy are mined under conditions that often involve environmental destruction, child labor, and conflict. Cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo and rare earth extraction in China illustrate the human and ecological costs.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: The green energy transition depends on these minerals. Ensuring ethical sourcing and recycling is critical to prevent clean technology from perpetuating exploitation and environmental harm.
takeaways: Rare earth mining often involves environmental devastation
Child labor and conflict fund some mineral supply chains
Recycling e-waste can reduce demand for new mining

faq.question: Why is cobalt mining controversial?
faq.answer: Over 70 percent of global cobalt comes from the DRC, where artisanal mines often use child labor in dangerous conditions. Workers dig by hand in unregulated tunnels with no safety equipment. Investigations have linked major electronics brands to these supply chains.

faq.question: Can recycling reduce the need for new mining?
faq.answer: Yes. Urban mining, which recovers metals from discarded electronics, can supply a growing share of demand. A smartphone contains over 30 elements. If global e-waste recycling rates doubled, it could significantly reduce pressure on primary extraction and associated harms.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Hazardous waste from industry, healthcare, and households includes chemicals, heavy metals, and radioactive materials that pose severe health risks. Improper disposal contaminates water, soil, and air, causing cancer, birth defects, and neurological damage in exposed communities worldwide.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Hazardous waste disproportionately harms low-income and marginalized communities. Proper management and regulation are essential for protecting public health and environmental justice.
takeaways: Hazardous waste includes chemicals, heavy metals, and radioactive material
Improper disposal causes cancer and neurological damage
Vulnerable communities bear the greatest health burden

faq.question: What counts as hazardous waste?
faq.answer: Waste is classified hazardous if it is ignitable, corrosive, reactive, or toxic. Examples include industrial solvents, pesticides, battery acid, medical sharps, asbestos, and electronics containing lead or mercury. Specific definitions vary by country and regulation.

faq.question: Where is hazardous waste most often dumped illegally?
faq.answer: Illegal dumping concentrates in countries with weak enforcement, often in Africa and Southeast Asia. The Probo Koala incident in 2006, where toxic waste from a Dutch company was dumped in Ivory Coast, sickened over 100,000 people and highlighted regulatory failures.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The fashion industry produces over 90 million tonnes of textile waste annually as fast fashion encourages frequent purchases of cheap, disposable clothing. Most discarded garments end up in landfills or are exported to developing countries, where much is burned or dumped rather than reused.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Fast fashion's waste footprint is enormous, yet largely invisible to consumers. Awareness of textile waste is driving demand for slower, more sustainable fashion models.
takeaways: Over 90 million tonnes of textile waste is produced yearly
Fast fashion promotes disposable consumption of clothing
Most discarded textiles end up in landfill or developing nations

faq.question: Where does donated clothing actually go?
faq.answer: Only about 10 to 20 percent of donated clothing is resold locally. The rest is exported to developing countries, where quality has declined as fast fashion saturates donations. Much ends up in open dumps rather than being worn, creating waste problems abroad.

faq.question: How can the fashion industry reduce textile waste?
faq.answer: Strategies include designing for durability, using recyclable mono-materials, implementing take-back programs, investing in fiber-to-fiber recycling technology, and shifting consumer culture toward quality over quantity. Extended producer responsibility legislation can drive systemic change.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Planned obsolescence is the practice of designing products to fail or become outdated within a set timeframe to drive repeat purchases. From non-replaceable batteries to software updates that slow old devices, manufacturers engineer limited lifespans that generate avoidable waste and consumer costs.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Planned obsolescence drives overproduction and waste at the design stage. Countering it through right-to-repair legislation and durable design is essential for a circular economy.
takeaways: Products are often designed to fail or become obsolete
Non-replaceable batteries and parts drive device disposal
Right-to-repair laws are emerging to counter the practice

faq.question: What are examples of planned obsolescence?
faq.answer: Smartphones with glued-in batteries, printers that stop working after a set number of pages, fashion seasons that make last year's clothing feel outdated, and software updates that slow older devices are all common examples of designed-in obsolescence.

faq.question: What is the right-to-repair movement?
faq.answer: Right-to-repair advocates for laws requiring manufacturers to provide parts, tools, and manuals so consumers and independent shops can fix products. The EU and several US states have passed or are considering such legislation, extending product lifespans and reducing waste.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Extended producer responsibility makes manufacturers responsible for the entire lifecycle of their products, including end-of-life collection and recycling. EPR programs funded by producer fees have dramatically increased recycling rates for packaging, electronics, and batteries in countries that adopt them.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: EPR shifts the cost of waste management from taxpayers to the companies that create the waste. This financial incentive drives manufacturers to design more recyclable and longer-lasting products.
takeaways: Producers pay for collection and recycling of their products
EPR incentivizes design for recyclability and durability
It has sharply increased recycling rates where implemented

faq.question: How does EPR work in practice?
faq.answer: Producers pay fees to compliance organizations based on the volume and type of products they sell. These organizations fund collection, sorting, and recycling infrastructure. Fees are higher for hard-to-recycle materials, incentivizing design changes.

faq.question: Which countries have the strongest EPR programs?
faq.answer: Germany pioneered packaging EPR in 1991. The EU now mandates EPR for packaging, electronics, and batteries. South Korea, Japan, and Canada also have robust programs. Coverage and effectiveness vary, with the best systems achieving recycling rates above 70 percent.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The circular economy replaces the linear take-make-dispose model with closed-loop systems where products are designed for reuse, repair, refurbishment, and recycling. It aims to keep materials in use as long as possible, extract maximum value, and regenerate natural systems instead of depleting them.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: A circular economy addresses waste and resource depletion at their root by redesigning how we produce and consume. It is fundamental to decoupling economic growth from environmental damage.
takeaways: The circular economy eliminates waste by design
Products are kept in use through repair, reuse, and recycling
It aims to decouple economic growth from resource consumption

faq.question: How does the circular economy differ from recycling?
faq.answer: Recycling is one tool within the circular economy, but circularity goes much further. It starts with designing products that last longer, can be repaired, and use fewer materials. Sharing, leasing, and refurbishment keep products in use. Recycling is the last resort, not the first.

faq.question: Is the circular economy economically viable?
faq.answer: The Ellen MacArthur Foundation estimates a circular economy could generate $4.5 trillion in economic value by 2030. Companies that adopt circular models often find new revenue streams from services, reduced material costs, and stronger customer loyalty.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Packaging-free stores sell food and household products in bulk, allowing customers to bring their own containers. They eliminate single-use packaging waste at the point of sale and encourage consumers to buy only what they need, reducing both packaging waste and food waste simultaneously.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Packaging accounts for a large share of household waste. Zero-waste stores demonstrate that retail can function without disposable packaging, inspiring broader systemic change.
takeaways: Customers bring containers and buy in exact quantities needed
Single-use packaging is eliminated at the point of sale
Buying only what is needed reduces food waste too

faq.question: Are packaging-free stores growing?
faq.answer: The sector has grown significantly since 2015, with thousands of stores now operating across Europe, North America, and Asia. Major supermarket chains have also begun adding refill sections. However, convenience and price competition with conventional packaging remain challenges.

faq.question: Is shopping without packaging hygienic?
faq.answer: Yes, when proper protocols are followed. Stores use gravity dispensers, tongs, and scoops. Containers are weighed empty before filling. Health regulations in most countries permit bulk selling with appropriate hygiene controls, much as bakeries and delis have always operated.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: Zero waste is a philosophy and strategy that aims to redesign resource cycles so that all products are reused, repaired, or recycled, and nothing is sent to landfills or incinerators. It is a systemic goal rather than a personal lifestyle, requiring changes across design, production, and policy.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Zero waste reframes the conversation from managing waste to preventing it. As a systemic goal, it drives innovation in product design, business models, and municipal waste policy.
takeaways: Zero waste aims to eliminate landfill and incineration entirely
It requires systemic change, not just individual action
Design for reuse and recyclability is the starting point

faq.question: Is zero waste actually achievable?
faq.answer: Perfect zero waste is an aspirational target, but many cities and businesses approach it. Kamikatsu, Japan, diverts over 80 percent of waste through 45 sorting categories. The goal drives continuous improvement even if absolute zero is practically impossible.

faq.question: What is the waste hierarchy?
faq.answer: The waste hierarchy ranks options from most to least preferred: prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and dispose. Zero waste focuses on the top of the hierarchy, prioritizing prevention and reduction over end-of-pipe solutions like recycling and incineration.

climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.summary: The United Nations is negotiating a Global Plastics Treaty aimed at reducing plastic pollution across the entire lifecycle, from production to disposal. If adopted, it would be the first legally binding international agreement addressing plastic pollution, setting global rules for reduction, recycling, and accountability.
climate-and-environment--waste-and-recyc.whyItMatters: Plastic pollution is a global problem that no single country can solve alone. A binding treaty could align international action and hold producers accountable for the full lifecycle of plastic products.
takeaways: Negotiations aim for a binding treaty covering plastic's full lifecycle
It would be the first global agreement specifically on plastic pollution
Debates center on whether to cap virgin plastic production

faq.question: What would the plastics treaty require?
faq.answer: Proposals range from capping virgin plastic production and banning problematic single-use items to mandating recycled content, funding waste management in developing countries, and establishing producer responsibility programs. The final scope depends on ongoing negotiations.

faq.question: When is the treaty expected to be finalized?
faq.answer: Negotiations began in 2022 with a target of completing the treaty by 2025. Progress has been slower than hoped due to disagreements between nations that want production limits and those that prefer focusing only on waste management downstream.
